openQuestions:
STRUCTURAL RESTORATION BLOCKED ON ROUTE ADJUDICATION, not an editorial judgment. The introduction to PART TWO, the running prose between the part label The Economic Architecture and the first chapter heading beneath it, compiles into a chapter-start section with its own public route. Restoring the baseline's fuller introduction revives a section whose route was retired, and the same hazard applies here even though this part did not break. The introduction has therefore been reverted to its pre-edit state byte for byte and no part introduction anywhere in this volume was touched. Reassigning a canonical route and a reviewed successor is an author-facing continuity decision and this pass has no standing to make it.

WHAT STANDS NOW:

Economic design cannot be postponed until after capital arrives. Funding terms, ownership, revenue, and measurement all shape what an institution can become.

Part II asks which forms of capital fit the constitutional principles, how value might circulate without a central extractor, and which resources must remain common. It offers design criteria, not proof that adequate compatible capital exists.

Saying that economics should serve the mission settles nothing. Ownership, contracts, incentives, and remedies determine whether the principle can survive pressure.

WHAT THE BASELINE HAS, punctuation already repaired so it can be pasted in one edit once the route decision is made:

Volume III deliberately deferred the economic question. The philosophical and constitutional foundations had to be established before the economic architecture could be built on them without being distorted by economic pressure. The deferral was honest, and consequential. An architecture whose economic design is determined by the funding environment rather than by the constitutional principles will, over time, be governed by the funding environment regardless of what the constitutional principles say.

The deferral ends here. Part II addresses the economic layer of Providence's architecture with the same depth that Volume III applied to the philosophical and constitutional layers. The questions it engages are not comfortable ones. How does an institution whose constitutional principles are incompatible with several of the most available forms of capital actually get capitalized? How does the internal economy of the institution reward what the constitutional principles establish as valuable rather than what the broader market environment rewards? How are the commons that the architecture depends on protected from enclosure as the institution grows and as economic pressure increases? What kinds of capital are structurally compatible with what Providence is trying to build, and what kinds are not, and how does the institution maintain this distinction when the incompatible forms of capital are more readily available than the compatible ones?

These are not questions that can be answered by stating the principle that economics must serve the mission rather than the other way around. Every institution with a social mission states that principle. The question is what institutional design makes it true rather than merely stated. Ownership, contracts, incentives, and remedies determine whether the principle can survive pressure. The four chapters of Part II attempt to answer that question with the specificity it requires. They offer design criteria, not proof that adequate compatible capital exists.

WHAT THE CURRENT TEXT LOSES: the account of why Volume III deferred the economic question and what the deferral cost, and the four questions the part sets itself, including how an institution whose principles are incompatible with the most available capital gets capitalized.

TO RESTORE: the prose change and the continuity change must land together. The section id minted by the restored introduction needs a canonical route and a reviewed successor recorded in publishing/continuity/section-lineage.json in the same edit.

The section's measured word count now exceeds the baseline's by a wide margin. This is a measurement artifact rather than an inflation: the damage tool splits on markdown headings, and with the coda headings gone this section absorbs the Part II opener that the baseline assigned to the coda. The same artifact affects six other sections in this volume.

The volume-04 voice card was prepared by the same pass that produced the shipped text, and its exemplar anchors and protected lines quote that text rather than the baseline. The card records `Author approved: pending tone, strategy, heading, and overcompression review`. The restoration keeps every line the card protects and otherwise follows the baseline, which means card and source now diverge in wording the card does not name. R-VOICE-BIND requires that the disagreement be raised rather than settled here: the card should be re-derived from whichever text the author approves.

Structural labels were frozen for this pass and none was touched. Every markdown heading, every standalone bold display line, every chapter label, and every all-capital display line is byte identical to its pre-edit state, in the same order, with the same blank-line separators on both sides. A label determines a section id, a section id is a public route, and `publishing/continuity/section-lineage.json` already records this volume's renames and resolves the historical routes. Changing one is a continuity decision and not an editorial one. Only the running prose between labels was restored. Where a baseline label names its section better than the current one, the cost is recorded here and the label is left alone.
